entries.title: The lordship of the manor
entries.narration: Llandough belongs to Tewkesbury Abbey until the Dissolution of 1536–39. Cardiff Records states that in 1543 Henry VIII granted the manor to Lord Clynton and Say and Robert Turwitt, and that by 1545 it was held by Sir George Herbert. The Western Mail letter says the Herberts held the lordship until the Earl of Bute bought it in 1793; Cardiff Records places William Hurst and others in the account from 1767. The same 1974 newspaper record identifies Mary (Nancy) Williams's family as occupying the manorial home since 1667. That occupation and the lordship are separate from the farmhouse freehold. The family's case is that the Williamses were virtual freeholders under the 1877 bargain while quarrying continued, and that Parcel A's freehold passed to them in 1928 when quarrying ended.

title_ledger.Great House (one farm): Lordship of the manor: Sir George Herbert (by 1545) and his family

entries.received_account: The lord of the manor owned the farm.

received_wording.note: The 1974 newspaper records the Williams family’s occupation of the manorial home; occupation is a separate matter from the lordship and the freehold.

entries.what_we_now_know: Lordship of a manor and ownership of the farmhouse parcel are separate interests. The 1974 newspaper records the Williams family’s occupation of the manorial home since 1667. The family’s title case is not occupation alone: it is that the 1877 bargain entitled the Williamses to Parcel A’s freehold when quarrying ended, identified by Mary as 1928, when the final rent was paid. On that account, the Williamses were virtual freeholders while the quarrying arrangement ran and became freeholders in 1928. The 1877 deed and final receipt have not been located, so the 1928 transfer remains the family’s asserted title history rather than a fact determined by the 1974 newspaper or a court. The manorial sources also differ over 1767–1793; the Herbert estate papers have not yet been checked.

entries.title: A 1,000-year lease of Cydwin
entries.narration: The National Library of Wales catalogue describes a lease for 1,000 years dated 20 June 1547 from Sir George Herbert of Swansea to Edmund Vaughan of a farm called Cydwin in the manor of Llandough; the record names fields. This long leasehold interest predates the later Bute estate narrative. The affirmative Cedwyn thesis asks whether those named fields belong to the older Cydfin/Ty Mawr holding later catalogued as a 107-acre farm, and how that interest passed from the Herbert/Vaughan line into subsequent estate records. The instrument and field boundaries must be examined before the lease can be equated with the whole Great House site.

entries.title: The Williams family at Great House

entries.title: The Bute Estate
entries.narration: The historical account places Bute's acquisition of the lordship of Llandough in 1793 and its acquisition of the Great House freehold in the early 19th century; the manorial courts of Llandough and Leckwith were held at the house. The missing control point is the instrument that carried the farm freehold from the Vaughan line into Bute's estate. The 1547 Cydwin lease, its 1739/40 assignment, and the D 219 record of Cydfin or Ty Mawr leases give the affirmative reconstruction a named chain to investigate alongside the manor's later ownership. A manorial interest, a long lease, and a farm freehold must be mapped separately before the later corporate titles can be treated as the originating chain for every parcel.

entries.received_account: Bute owned the farm, and everything after descends from Bute.
entries.what_we_now_know: The historical account places the manorial lordship in Bute's hands from 1793 and the Great House farm freehold in the early 19th century. The deed that moved the farm freehold from the Vaughan line is the key missing control point. The L 11 lease assignment and D 219 farm records provide older property and tenure references against which Bute's acquisition, rentals and subsequent 1877 division must be tested. The house was also a centre for the Llandough and Leckwith manorial courts; that administrative role must not be confused with ownership of each parcel.

entries.title: "Williams John, Great house"
entries.narration: The trade directories list the farmers of Llandough parish. Every edition from 1868 to 1901 has "Williams John, Great house", from 1887 "Great House farm, Llandough". Thomas Rees, and later Evan Rees, are listed separately, at Llandough Farm, a different Bute farm.

entries.what_we_now_know: Six directories over 33 years put the same John Williams at Great House and the Rees family at Llandough Farm, so the two farms, and the two families, were distinct. Against it: directories copy from one edition to the next and record what the compiler was told; none uses the name "Home Farm"; and the press of 1895 and 1904 sometimes calls a Williams "of Llandough Farm", so that name in a source does not always mean the Rees farm.

entries.title: A Williams estate bequest to Bute: tracing the land
entries.narration: The National Library of Wales catalogue lists the 1870 will of William Evans Williams of Pwllypant as bequeathing his real and personal estate to the Marquis of Bute, and separately catalogues papers about his real and personal estate. The affirmative title inquiry is parcel-specific: did any land he owned, benefited from, or had let through Bute connect to the 33-acre Llandough Limeworks block or Great House Farm? The will's headline bequest does not identify those acres by itself. The family's research also points to a Clock Tower dispute and newspaper coverage said to complicate the relationship between Williams and Bute; the precise contemporary reports and wording must be located before using that dispute as proof of motive. Estate schedules, title deeds, rent books and the 1876–1912 limeworks accounts are the route to answer the question.

entries.place: Glamorgan County Council planning committee, Cardiff
entries.narration: Mary (Nancy) Williams, as Mrs M. D. Buckler, objects to Glamorgan County Council's planning committee about industrial development beside Tŷ Mawr. The Western Mail reports that land "farmed by her family since 1667" had been "wrongfully appropriated", that "This is a Welsh case of Crichel Down", that "the water was cut off from her house and grounds for nearly 10 years by order of Western Ground Rents", and that "The Glamorgan County Council, Penarth Urban and Cardiff Rural Councils and Western Ground Rents have walked in and taken" (the search text ends there).

entries.what_we_now_know: The only record of the time so far that the water was cut off: Mrs Buckler's own claim in 1958, as the Western Mail reported it. It names the landlord, Western Ground Rents, not a council. Crichel Down (1954) was the national scandal over farmland the state kept after requisition; a minister resigned over it. "Nearly 10 years" would put the start around 1948–49 (an inference). Per Branwen Buckler (voice testimony, relayed by Sion Buckler, 19 October 2026), the council cut the water over bills it said were unpaid, which Mary (Nancy) Williams insisted had been paid; dairy cattle drowned in the River Ely trying to reach water, a baby daughter had to live elsewhere, and the matter was raised in Parliament. What cuts against that version: the 1958 report names Western Ground Rents, not a council or a water bill; no report of cattle drowning has been found; no Commons or Lords debate or written answer has been found for 1946–92 (committee proceedings and MPs' letters are not searchable this way); and Dŵr Cymru's 2026 replies speak of a disconnection in the 1980s, so there may have been two cut-offs. The article has been read only as search snippets; the full page is still to be obtained.

entries.title: Amalgamation of titles
entries.narration: On 2 February 1987, while the appeal is pending, an application is made to amalgamate WA240304 (the separately registered farmhouse and garden) into WA231076 (the larger field title). entries.received_account: A landlord and its successors recovered their farm from tenants who stayed on without paying, and the courts confirmed it.
entries.what_we_now_know: Parcel A was the family's from 1928, and by possession from 1940. It was never shown to belong to Western Ground Rents or BP. A synthetic single farm was described in 1916; six attempts (1949, 1955, 1959, 1962, 1965, 1974) treated Mary's occupation as permissive; the woodland and the land to the south were taken; the 1975 conveyance and 1983 registration gave the synthetic Parcel A a deed and a title; the 1987 amalgamation folded it into Parcel B. The courts decided possession and never decided ownership. Possession can be awarded without ownership being tried, and land can be registered without a rival claim being decided. Neither decides the older title.

entries.what_we_now_know: Mary's 1974 statement describes the 1877 split; no lawyer of hers built a case on it. Western Ground Rents offered tenancies of, and sued for, the farmhouse and garden alone. BP conveyed it alone in 1975, registered it alone in 1983, and merged it in 1987. The Land Registry held two titles and joined them. The Court of Appeal read a conveyance of the farmhouse and garden. Those who knew the parcels were separate treated them as one where that helped and as two where that helped. The family's case is that this was a conspiracy against them.
